We make lead time the primary evaluation object with a latch-on-resistant, false-alarm-gated metric: warning time counts only when the pre-onset false-alarm rate is within a budget τ , so a constant-on detector is provably invalid.
With it we test whether a SCADA historian’s bin-averaged logging destroys lead time relative to decimation.

Condition-based maintenance (CBM) and prognostics and health management (PHM) replace fixed-interval servicing with data-driven intervention, reducing both unplanned downtime and unnecessary maintenance (Jardine, Lin, & Banjevic, 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2018).

Rollingelement bearings are the most common failure mode in rotating machinery, and statistical control charts, classical machine learning and deep models are all used to detect incipient bearing faults from vibration (Randall & Antoni, 2011; Zhao et al., 2019).
A warning delivered hours or days before a catastrophic seizure lets an operator schedule an orderly shutdown, order parts and avoid secondary damage to shafts, housings and couplings.

Yet most published detectors are evaluated with classification metrics—accuracy, precision/recall and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC)—which answer “was the failure detected?” but not the planner’s question: “how many hours of warning did we get, and how often did the system cry wolf?
A detector that warns 48 h ahead at a low nuisance-alarm rate is operationally distinct from one that fires minutes before breakdown or one that alarms every day.

Time-aware prognostic metrics have long been advocated (Saxena et al., 2008; Saxena, Celaya, Saha, Saha, & Goebel, 2010; Goebel, Saha, & Saxena, 2011), yet lead time is rarely the headline quantity in detector benchmarks, and ad hoc definitions are easy to game: without a false-alarm constraint, a detector that alarms from the first sample—a “latchon” exploit—earns the full run length as lead time while being operationally useless.
A second question is practical.

Industrial Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) historians rarely store raw high-rate vibration; they keep decimated or time-averaged summaries at a logging interval of seconds to minutes (Tautz-Weinert & Watson, 2017), not the tens of kilohertz at which accelerometers sample.

The folklore concern is that bin-averaging these summaries washes out the excursions that signal an incipient spall, so that long-term storage would blind any prognostic algorithm that consumes the historian.
To our knowledge this has not been tested with a sound lead-time metric across multiple datasets.

If averaging is harmless, operators can store compact, cheap, bin-averaged streams without sacrificing warning time; if it is harmful, prognostics-grade monitoring requires separate high-rate acquisition.
We answer both questions.
Lead time gated by a leakage-free pre-onset false-alarm rate is the primary metric, so the latchon detector is provably scored invalid rather than winning.

Scope of claims.

The results are for rolling-element bearings under approximately steady operating conditions; we make no claim of transfer to gearboxes, blades or variablespeed machinery, and the sampling question is specifically bin-averaged versus decimated historian storage.
The metric itself is failure-mode-agnostic: it applies wherever a run-tofailure trajectory and a stationary normal region exist.
Our working hypothesis was that bin-averaging the stored summary series would wash out incipient-fault excursions and shorten lead time.
It does not, and we report the refutation, with its dataset-dependent direction explicit, as more valuable than a tidy but unsupported positive claim.

Reviews of machinery diagnostics and prognostics (Jardine et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2018) and of remaininguseful-life (RUL) estimation (Si, Wang, Hu, & Zhou, 2011) establish the CBM/PHM framing in which a health indicator is tracked and an alarm or RUL estimate is produced.
Saxena et al.
(2008), Saxena et al.
(2010) and Goebel et al.
(2011) propose prognostic-performance metrics (prognostic horizon, α-λ accuracy, relative accuracy and timeliness) that reward early, well-calibrated predictions.
Our onset-relative lead time is in this spirit: it measures warning time relative to a degradation event, not an arbitrary positional marker.

We depart from prior practice by making the false-alarm budget part of the metric’s validity condition rather than a separately reported number, which closes the latch-on loophole, and we give what is to our knowledge the first formal comparison showing that an ungated prognostic horizon ranks detectors differently, and misleadingly, from a false-alarmbudgeted metric (Section 6.11).
The cost asymmetry between a missed detection and a false alarm has been treated explicitly outside bearing prognostics.

The Numenta Anomaly Benchmark (Lavin & Ahmad, 2015) scores streaming detectors under an application profile that rewards early detection and penalises false positives, making our gate’s commitment in another domain: earliness cannot be assessed independently of nuisance-alarm behaviour.
The difference is structural.

That benchmark folds both into one weighted score, so a detector may trade false alarms against earliness and still rank well; our budget is a validity condition, and an alarm outside it earns no credit that a longer lead can offset.
A parallel line of work revises evaluation itself for time-series detection.

Tatbul, Lee, Zdonik, Alam, and Gottschlich (2018) generalise precision and recall from points to ranges with a tunable positional bias, so early detection within an anomalous interval can be rewarded, and Wu and Keogh (2023) argue that widely used benchmarks admit trivial solutions and overstate progress.

Our metric shares the diagnosis but reports a physical quantity—hours of warning—that a planner can act on, rather than a score on a bounded scale, and the false-alarm constraint gates validity rather than weighting the score.

Univariate and multivariate statistical-process-control charts—the 3σ rule, the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) (Roberts, 1959) and Hotelling’s T 2 (Hotelling, 1947)—remain workhorses of industrial monitoring (Montgomery, 2009) because they are interpretable and need little training data.

Isolation Forest (Liu, Ting, & Zhou, 2008) and the one-class SVM (Schölkopf, Platt, ShaweTaylor, Smola, & Williamson, 2001) are widely deployed unsupervised learners; LSTM autoencoders (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997; Malhotra et al., 2016; Hundman, Constantinou, Laporte, Colwell, & Soderstrom, 2018) and Deep SVDD (Ruff et al., 2018) have been applied to machine-health monitoring (Zhao et al., 2019).
We evaluate both families under one fixed hyperparameter protocol, so the comparison is about evaluation and sampling, not tuning.
Relation to published FEMTO/XJTU results.

The IEEE PHM 2012 challenge and later remaining-useful-life (RUL) studies on FEMTO/PRONOSTIA and XJTU-SY (Wang, Lei, Li, & Li, 2020; Nectoux et al., 2012) report a RUL-error score on deliberately truncated Test and Validation copies.

The IEEE PHM 2012 challenge and later remaining-useful-life (RUL) studies on FEMTO/PRONOSTIA and XJTU-SY (Wang, Lei, Li, & Li, 2020; Nectoux et al., 2012) report a RUL-error score on deliberately truncated Test and Validation copies.

It is not comparable to ours: they estimate a continuous RUL on runs with no observed failure and report no false-alarm rate, so their scores say nothing about whether an alarm would survive our τ gate, whereas we measure early-warning lead time on complete run-to-failure trajectories; tabulating one against the other would be a category error.

The classic normalized-RMS health indicator with a first-prediction-time threshold, the baseline underlying most of that literature, is our rms_trend detector; re-evaluating specific published architectures under the gated metric (which requires their original code) is future work.
The pairing of detection delay with a false-alarm constraint is the founding formulation of sequential change detection.

Lorden (1971) posed the minimax problem of minimising worst-case detection delay subject to a lower bound on the average run length to false alarm, Moustakides (1986) showed that the cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart of Page (1954) is exactly optimal under that criterion, and Pollak (1985) gives the corresponding result for a revised delay measure.
Our gate inherits the premise but applies it when a detector is scored, against a rate measured on the data, rather than when it is designed by choosing a threshold that meets a run-length bound.

Uncertainty Quantification and Conformal Prediction

Conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman, & Shafer, 2005; Laxhammar & Falkman, 2014) bounds the false-alarm rate by a target α under exchangeability, converting a raw score into an alarm with an interpretable, finite-sample guarantee.

We wire conformal calibration into the lead-time pipeline and test the guarantee empirically across runs, including a run where exchangeability provably fails because the “normal” region already contains degradation.
Bearing-defect frequencies, spectral kurtosis (Antoni, 2006) and envelope (demodulation) analysis (Randall & Antoni, 2011) are the classical frequency-domain tools for bearing diagnostics.

We include fast Fourier transform (FFT) band energies, spectral kurtosis and Hilbert-envelope amplitudes at the bearing characteristic frequencies, and ablate them against time-domain statistics to see which family carries prognostic lead time under the gated metric.

Tautz-Weinert and Watson (2017) review SCADA-data condition monitoring and note that historian aggregation is a recognized but under-quantified concern: practitioners suspect that coarse averaging hurts fault detection, but the effect has not been measured with a principled warning-time metric.
We address this gap and find that, for bearing faults, the concern is not borne out.

The headline set comprises nine detectors under one fixed hyperparameter protocol: an RMS-trend naive baseline, which alarms when the mean RMS exceeds kσ above its training baseline and is included to verify that the metric penalizes a weak detector; the 3σ rule, alarming when the ℓ2-norm health index exceeds three training standard deviations; an EWMA chart (Roberts, 1959) (λ = 0.2, k = 3.0), sensitive to small sustained shifts; a deterministic two-sided tabular CUSUM chart (Page, 1954) (k = 0.5, h = 5.0) on the monitored magnitude, the classic change-point chart most sensitive to a small sustained mean shift such as slow degradation onset; Hotelling T 2 (Hotelling, 1947) in a principal component analysis (PCA)-reduced subspace (rank ≪ n), so the covariance is well-conditioned; Isolation Forest (Liu et al., 2008), an unsupervised ensemble that isolates anomalies with few random splits; and three deep reconstruction baselines—an LSTM autoencoder (Malhotra et al., 2016), a temporal convolutional network autoencoder (dilated causal convolutions) and a lightweight reconstruction Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017)—each trained on normal feature-window sequences only and scoring a window by its reconstruction error.

The comparison is not straightforward—RUL methods predict a remaining-life quantity and are scored by prediction error, whereas our metric scores when an alarm fires against a false-alarm budget—but the consequence is that the metric’s behaviour relative to that body of work is untested, and readers coming from RUL benchmarking should treat the two as complementary rather than ranked.
